```{r setup, message=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)
```


```{r problem 1}
data("ny_noaa")
glimpse(ny_noaa)
colSums(is.na(ny_noaa))
colMeans(is.na(ny_noaa)) * 100
```
The ny_noaa dataset depicts the weather of each stations from 1981 to 2010. There are 7 variables and 2595176 rows of dataset. "date" is the date of a weather record. "prcp" is the precipitation on this day.
"snow" and "snwd" describe the snow amount and depth on this certain day. "tmax" and "tmin" are the max and min temperature of the day, respectively.
Missing data are a substantial concern in this dataset, particularly for temperature: approximately 43.71% of observations are missing for each of tmax and tmin. Missingness is also present in snwd (22.80%), snow (14.69%), and prcp (5.62%), while id and date have no missing values. These missing values reduce the available data for analysis and may introduce bias if missingness varies systematically across stations or time periods

```{r problem 1 question 1}
#problem 1 question 1
ny_noaa_clean = ny_noaa |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(
    year = lubridate::year(date),
    month = lubridate::month(date),
    day = lubridate::day(date),
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax)/10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin)/10,
    prcp = prcp/10
  ) 

ny_noaa_clean |>
  filter(!is.na(snow)) |>
  count(snow)
```
0 is the most frequent number of snowfall. Because in the observed areas, most days of the year are not snowing.

```{r problem 1 question 2}
#problem 1 question 2
temp_summary = ny_noaa_clean |>
  filter(month == 1| month == 7) |>
  group_by(id, month, year) |>
  summarise(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

temp_summary |>
  filter(!is.na(mean_tmax)) |>
    mutate(
    month = factor(
      month,
      levels = c(1, 7),
      labels = c("January", "July")
    )
  ) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)) + 
  geom_line(alpha = 0.2) +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y =  "Highest temperature of the day" 
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
The plot shows year-to-year fluctuations in average maximum temperature. There are repeated rises and falls, there seems to have a regular rise-fall pattern over 4 to 5 years. A potential outlier appears in July around 1988.


```{r problem 1 question 3}
#problem 1 question 3
p1 = ny_noaa_clean |>
  filter(!is.na(tmax),!is.na(tmin)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_bin_2d() +
  labs(
    x = "Minimum temperature (°C)",
    y = "Maximum temperature (°C)",
    fill = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

p2 = ny_noaa_clean |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = snow)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Snowfall"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
  axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5)
)

library(patchwork)
p1 + p2
```

```{r problem 2}
#problem 2
#load and merge dataset
accel_df = read_csv(
  file = "data/nhanes_accel.csv",
  na = c("",".","NA") 
) |>
  janitor::clean_names()

covar_df = read_csv(
  file = "data/nhanes_covar.csv",
  na = c("",".","NA"),
  skip = 4
) |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(
    sex = case_when(
      sex == 1 ~ "male",
      sex == 2 ~ "female",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    education = case_when(
      education == 1 ~ "Less than high school",
      education == 2 ~ "High school equivalent",
      education == 3 ~ "More than high school",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
    ) |>
  filter(age >= 21) |>
  drop_na(bmi, education, age)  |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(
      sex,
      levels = c("male", "female")
    ),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(
        "Less than high school",
        "High school equivalent",
        "More than high school"
      )
    )
  )

nhanes_df = covar_df |>
  left_join(accel_df, by = "seqn")

#create table
nhanes_df |>
  count(sex, education) |>
  pivot_wider(  
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    caption = "Number of participants by education and sex"
  )

nhanes_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = sex, y = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_grid(.~education) +
  labs(
    x = "Sex",
    y = "Age",
    title = "Age distributions by sex and education"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
Among male and female participants, more than high school is the category with most people, which have 59 and 56 individuals respectively. The number of men who has high school equivalent diploma is dramatically greater than women. For distributions, high school equivalent participants category has a remarkable difference for female and male, in which male has a much lower median age in this category. For the other two education levels, the distributions of sex are similar generally.

```{r problem 2 activity plot}
#problem 2 activity plot
#plot of total activity
nhanes_df |>
  mutate(
    total_activity = rowSums(across(min1:min1440), na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_grid(.~education) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    x = "age",
    y = "Total Activity",
    title = "Total Activity vs. Age across different education levels"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
Total daily activity generally decreases with age across all three education categories. Men tend to have lower activity levels than women in the less than high school and more than high school groups. The more than high school group shows the slowest decline in activity with age.

```{r problem 2 24 hour activity}
#problem 2 24 hour activity
#plot of 24 hour activity
activity_long = nhanes_df |>
    pivot_longer(
      cols = min1:min1440,
      names_to = "minute",
      names_prefix = "min",
      names_transform = list(minute = as.integer),
      values_to = "activity",
    )

activity_avg = activity_long |>
  group_by(education, sex, minute) |>
  summarise(
    mean_activity = mean(activity)
  )

activity_avg |>
  ggplot(aes(x = minute/60, y = mean_activity, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  facet_grid(.~education) + 
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.5) +
  labs(
    x = "Hour",
    y = "Mean Activity",
    title = "24-hour activity time courses"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Across all three education levels, daily activity follows a similar pattern. Activity levels are lowest during the early morning hours (around 3–5 AM), increase rapidly after 6 AM, and remain relatively high throughout the daytime before declining in the evening.
Females generally exhibit slightly higher activity levels than males during the day, particularly among individuals with a high school education or less. The less than high school group shows the highest morning activity peak, while the more than high school group maintains relatively stable activity levels throughout the daytime.

```{r problem 3}
#problem 3
Jan2024_df = read_csv(
  file = "data/Jan 2024 Citi.csv",
  na = c("",".","NA")
) |>
  janitor::clean_names() 

Jan2020_df = read_csv(
  file = "data/Jan 2020 Citi.csv",
  na = c("",".","NA")
) |>
  janitor::clean_names() 

July2020_df = read_csv(
  file = "data/July 2020 Citi.csv",
  na = c("",".","NA")
) |>
  janitor::clean_names() 

July2024_df = read_csv(
  file = "data/July 2024 Citi.csv",
  na = c("",".","NA")
) |>
  janitor::clean_names() 

citibike_df = bind_rows(
  Jan2020_df |> mutate(year = 2020, month = "January"),
  July2020_df |> mutate(year = 2020, month = "July"),
  Jan2024_df |> mutate(year = 2024, month = "January"),
  July2024_df |> mutate(year = 2024, month = "July")
)

#table of rides separating riders
citibike_df |>
  group_by(year, month, member_casual) |>
  summarise(
    ride_count = n(), 
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = member_casual,
    values_from = ride_count
  ) 

#5 most popular starting stations for July 2024
citibike_df |>
  filter(year == 2024, month == "July") |>
  group_by(start_station_name) |>
  summarise(
    ride_count = n()
  ) |>
  filter(min_rank(desc(ride_count)) <= 5) |>
  knitr::kable()

#Plot to investigate the effects of day of the week, month, and year on median ride duration
citibike_median = citibike_df |>
  group_by(weekdays, year, month) |>
  summarise(
    median_dur = median(duration),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

citibike_median = citibike_median |>
  mutate(
    weekdays = factor(
      weekdays,
      levels = c(
        "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday",
        "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"
      )
    )
  )

plot_1 = citibike_median |>
  ggplot(aes(x = weekdays, y = median_dur, color = month, group = month)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_grid(.~year) +
  labs(
    x = "day of the week",
    y = "median duration",
    color = "Month",
    title = "Median Ride Duration by Weekday, Month, and Year"
  ) + 
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
  axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
)
  plot_1
            
```
Median ride duration is consistently higher in July than in January across both years. Rides also tend to be longer on weekends than on weekdays, particularly in 2020. Overall, median ride duration decreased from 2020 to 2024, with a more substantial decline in July. Additionally, the gap between January and July narrowed considerably in 2024, suggesting a reduction in seasonal differences in ride duration.

```{r problem 3 last part}
#problem 3 last part
citibike_df |>
  filter(year == 2024) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = month, y = duration, color = member_casual)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_grid(.~rideable_type) +
  labs(
    x = "Month",
    y = "Duration",
    color = "Member Type",
    title = "Impact of month, membership status, and bike type(2024)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Across both months and bike types, casual riders generally have longer median ride durations than Citi Bike members. This difference is particularly pronounced for classic bikes. Ride durations also tend to be longer in July than in January, although the magnitude of this difference varies across groups. Casual riders using classic bikes generally have longer rides than those using electric bikes, while the difference between bike types is smaller among members. Additionally, ride duration distributions are right-skewed, with numerous high-duration outliers across all groups.
